item.title: Ball-tampering row: Pat Cummins invites media, to address 'long list and full extent' of Usman Khawaja's allegations
item.description: Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is set to respond to Usman Khawaja's allegations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, saying he needed time to understand the claims made in the former opener's autobiography before addressing them. Khawaja's book, 'Sabr', released on Tuesday, has brought the controversy surrounding the Cape Town Test against South Africa in 2018 back into focus. In the book, Khawaja claimed that the entire Australian team knew about the plan to use sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball. He also alleged that then captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Cameron Bancroft were made scapegoats by cricket administrators despite other members of the team allegedly knowing about the plan. Cummins said he would address the media on Friday at Cricket Central, where he is scheduled to train ahead of New South Wales' Sheffield Shield match. "I'm training at Cricket Central tomorrow morning before the Blues play in the Shield match," Cummins wrote on 'X'. "Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week at 9.30 am. I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly." Khawaja, meanwhile, has withdrawn from interviews to promote his autobiography after facing criticism over his television interview on Tuesday evening. During the interview, he struggled to address questions about the allegations, including whether Australia's four frontline bowlers, Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, were involved in discussions about ball-tampering. He was also directly asked whether Cummins knew about the plan to use sandpaper in advance. Khawaja declined to answer, saying he had only shared his "truth" in the book. Former Australia captain Michael Clarke has also questioned Cummins' silence on the matter, saying the team needs to establish what happened during the 2018 Test. Speaking on 2DayFM's Breakfast with Nath & Emma, Clarke expressed surprise that the current Australia captain had not yet addressed the allegations publicly. "I can't believe we haven't heard from Pat Cummins yet, the Australian captain," Clarke said. Clarke also pointed to the impact of the 2018 scandal on Australian cricket's leadership, suggesting that Cummins might not have become captain had Smith not been removed from the role following the incident.

item.title: Ten years, three kids later - Oliva back for Olympic bid
item.description: Oliva (second from left) won Commonwealth bronze for Team Wales as part of the women's team pursuit in Glasgow [Getty Images] Cyclist and mum-of-three Ciara Oliva says she has 'unfinished business' at the Olympics after making a remarkable return to the British Cycling programme. The former European champion and world bronze medallist spent almost a decade out of the sport and has three children with partner and fellow cyclist, Lewis. But after missing out on final selection to compete at the Rio 2016 Games, the 37-year-old admits she just could not give up on her Olympic dream. She returned to international competition at the summer's Commonwealth Games, winning bronze for Wales in the women's team pursuit, but says that was only the start. "I could have stopped there," she told BBC Sport Wales. "It felt like one of the most magical moments. My favourite medal I've ever had internationally, winning a bronze medal with the girls in the team pursuit in front of my children. It was like a fairytale ending in itself. "But there's unfinished business and I am going to chase my Olympic dream one last time." Horne's Rio dream inspired by scrapbook Olympic heartache fuels Oliva's comeback Oliva first joined the Great Britain cycling programme in 2014. She won bronze at the 2016 World Championships as part of the women's team pursuit. She also won two European titles in the same event. But come the Rio 2016 Olympics, Oliva was left watching on as reserve. Laura Kenny, Katie Archibald, Elinor Barker and Joanna Rowsell were chosen for the Olympic team pursuit - and they smashed the world record to take gold. "The fastest team rode," she is happy to admit. "They won gold. "But I had to stand on the sidelines and watch that happen. And I was truly heartbroken." Oliva retired in 2018 and went on to be a physiotherapist - "I honestly thought I was done". "People would mention cycling and I would discuss it, but I always found it hard to talk about the Olympics. I got so close and yet so far," she reflected. "The years went by and I had my three beautiful children, but I watched Helen Glover's documentary and I just burst into tears. I was like, I'm not done yet. "There was still that little voice that was saying, just have a crack at it one last time. "So to now have an opportunity to chase this, but this time with my family, my children by my side, watching mummy do all this crazy training day in day out, has just made the journey so much more special than I thought was even possible." item.title: Manchester United reportedly sack Michael Carrick with Pochettino in line
item.description: Manchester United reportedly sack Michael Carrick with Pochettino in line Manchester United reportedly sack Michael Carrick as Mauricio Pochettino nears Old Trafford job Manchester United have sacked Michael Carrick, according to reports, with Mauricio Pochettino expected to replace him before the Premier League trip to Liverpool on 22 November. Cameron Smith, writing for FootballTransfers , cited Fabrizio Romano and The Athletic in reporting that United had decided to dismiss Carrick with immediate effect. At the time of publication on Thursday morning, United had yet to formally announce his departure or appoint a successor. Carrick’s final fixture was a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. A late equaliser salvaged a point at Old Trafford, but United went into the November international break in 18th place, with eight points from their opening ten league matches. IMAGO Carrick’s permanent spell falls short of his interim promise As recently as May, United had good reason to believe Carrick was the right man for the job. His work as interim manager had persuaded the club to give him the position permanently. Less than six months later, he leaves with fewer wins in all competitions this season than United managed goals in his final match. Across 15 fixtures, Carrick’s side won three, drew five and lost seven. One of those wins, against Roma in the Champions League, offered a glimpse of why his players could still command a crowd at Old Trafford. Yet European results could do nothing to improve a league position that had come to define his tenure. Bournemouth defeat put Carrick’s job in doubt The 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth in late October marked a turning point. According to FootballTransfers, Carrick was given three games to save his job. Two of the responses that followed were memorable for much the same reason: United found themselves in trouble and had enough attacking quality to recover. Against Roma, a Bruno Fernandes penalty and two goals from Matheus Cunha turned a two-goal half-time deficit into a 3-2 victory. Against Villa, United went one better in front of goal and still came away with less. Scoring four at home earned them a single Premier League point. There was evidence in those games that the players could respond to Carrick under pressure. What was missing, particularly against Villa, was the ability to put themselves in a position where a rescue act was unnecessary. Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann, Antonio Conte and Unai Emery had also been linked with the position, but it is the former Tottenham and Chelsea manager whom FootballTransfers identifies as the expected appointment. item.title: Opportunity knocked. Louisville WR TreyShun Hurry responded in big way
item.description: For the past two years, TreyShun Hurry has played two kinds of games: football games and the waiting game. After transferring from San Jose State to Louisville in 2025, the wide receiver became a starter for the Cardinals. But he was overshadowed by Chris Bell and Caullin Lacy, and limited to 122 yards and a touchdown on 15 receptions. During the offseason, UofL added Vanderbilt transfer Tre Richardson and Florida State transfer Lawayne McCoy , who were expected to be a three-headed threat with Hurry. "Last year he was playing X, he was on the backside, really didn't see the ball too much and was just trying to kind of feel his way through the season," wide receivers coach Deion Branch said about Hurry during fall camp. "He got better and better week in, week out. But now here's the opportunity for him to possibly be one of the main guys." Hurry maintained his starting position entering this season, but McCoy and Richardson became the stars of the Cards' passing offense . They were the main options, and again, Hurry waited. McCoy got hurt against Syracuse on Oct. 17 and is out indefinitely. That opened the door for Hurry to get some of those looks. It was never about Hurry's ability, only opportunity. With it, he has taken advantage. Two weeks ago, he caught his second touchdown pass as a Card. Last week at Georgia Tech, he matched his career-high with eight receptions for a 104 yards and another score. Hurry enters the Nov. 14 game at North Carolina second on the team in receptions (39) and third in yards (474). "We're missing a big piece of our offense," Hurry said of McCoy. "So I just had to step up, and so it's no drop-off for the team and stay explosive.” Hurry had seven catches for 107 yards through the first three games of the season. But over the past three games, he's had 203 yards and two touchdowns on 15 receptions. His first touchdown of the season came on a 22-yard catch from Lincoln Kienholz in Louisville's 52-24 win over Stanford on Oct. 31. Kienholz might have been just as excited as Hurry, if not more so. "I think he's a super solid receiver," the quarterback said. "He gets open when he needs to. If you go back and just look at his games, he's had multiple games with 60-plus receiving yards, which is huge. ... That's something I was driving to try to get him his first one (touchdown)." Hurry followed that performance with a career day against Georgia Tech . The California native hadn't had a 100-yard receiving game since he was with Weber State in 2023. item.title: Key part of Kentucky football's passing game has yet to be unlocked
item.description: LEXINGTON — By many measures, Kentucky football 's Kenny Minchey has been among the best quarterbacks in the SEC — and the country at large — this fall. He enters this week just outside the top 10 in the FBS in completion percentage (69.9). He averages nearly 21 completions per game, which ranks third in the conference. And he's kept interceptions to a minimum, with just two all season; only Missouri's Austin Simmons has thrown more passes (283) than Minchey (266) among SEC signal callers while totaling only two INTs. But for all of Minchey's success, one reason for his efficiency is he's feasted on short throws. Per Pro Football Focus , Minchey has completed 80.8% (84 for 104) of his "short passes," which are defined of throws between 0 and 9 yards. He's even more accurate behind the line of scrimmage, where he's connected on 94.4% (67 for 71) of his screen attempts. It's a different story on longer tosses. Minchey is 24 for 42 (57.1%) on "medium passes," which are throws between 10 and 19 yards. And on deep throws — those of 20 yards or longer — he's just 11 of 31 (35.5%). Just three of his completions this season have covered 40 or more yards. For context, 15 quarterbacks nationally have at least 10 such completions, including SEC leader Arch Manning and Louisville's Lincoln Kienholz. It must be noted, of course, that the farther the throw, the higher the level of difficulty. Not to mention the fact defenders have more time to react to a ball in the air as opposed to one that doesn't even cross the line of scrimmage. His teammates haven't been perfect hauling in those aforementioned long throws, as the Wildcats are credited with two drops. (The walk-in touchdown freshman wide receiver Kenny Darby dropped at Texas A&M is the most glaring example.) Yet Minchey hasn't helped himself at times, either. Of his 31 deep throws, he has a Turnover Worthy Play Rate of 9.4%. PFF defines a Turnover Worthy Play as "a pass that has a high percentage chance to be intercepted or a poor job of taking care of the ball and fumbling." Minchey's percentage ranks 30th nationally . It's the second-worst percentage in the conference; only Arkansas' KJ Jackson has been more risky at 11.6%. The numbers don't lie: Minchey has been well-below average on deep throws. His PFF grade of 66.1 is tied for 130th of the 156 FBS quarterbacks evaluated by the site. That ranked above only two of his SEC colleagues: Auburn's Byrum Brown at 58.9 and Jackson (again) at 52.5. item.title: His days on oil rigs are done. Spence Nowinsky strikes it rich with New Mexico football
item.description: Before Spence Nowinsky built college football ’s stingiest defense, he was running through airports, inspecting storage tanks and checking gas dispensers for leaks. Football had spit him out. After a coaching change at Idaho left Nowinsky without a job, the former Minnesota State defensive lineman took work with a compliance company servicing the oil industry. The money was good. The football prospects weren’t. Then came a chance to get back in. “I think I took a $150,000 haircut to go coach football again.” CFB Unfiltered: What the CFP rankings got wrong about Indiana, Miami More than two decades later, that decision looks like one hell of an investment. Nowinsky is the architect of a New Mexico defense allowing a meager 10.89 points per game, the backbone of one of college football’s most improbable transformations under Jason Eck. The Lobos have won 17 of Eck’s first 22 games, including 14 of their past 16, and cracked the US LBM Coaches and AP polls for the first time in school history. Getting from the oil industry to Albuquerque, though, requires more than an atlas. The story traces almost 1,200 miles northeast, far closer to International Falls than New Mexico, to Mankato, Minnesota. There, at Minnesota State, the threads connecting Eck, Nowinsky and Lobos offensive coordinator Luke Schleusner began forming at different times, on different paths, before ultimately converging in Albuquerque. The plucky NCAA Division II football program is playing a disproportionate role in college football across the country this season, but especially at New Mexico, where Eck, who might be the hottest name in college football coaching circles right now, drives lowriders, fraternizes with fans as an everyman and suddenly sells out University Stadium. A former Wisconsin lineman, Eck does all of this with a modest operating budget, a different athletic director than the one who hired him two years ago and an unrelenting, uncompromising defense. Enter Nowinsky. He arrived to find one of the nation’s leakiest defenses, the No. 130 scoring unit in 2024. He helped reduce that figure to 22 points per game a year ago, then nearly halved it to claim the nation’s top spot through the first 10 weeks of this season. It’s a remarkable rise for a coach who once ran contracts for oil rigs in the nascent days of his yet-to-lift-off career and now operates college football’s stingiest defense. “It wasn’t on the patch and that type of thing, I worked for a compliance company, above ground and below ground checking storage tanks, is it leaking, are your gas dispensers in proper working condition," the barrel-chested Nowinsky says. "I literally traveled every single day, running through airports catching planes. It was ridiculous but I got an opportunity to then go back to Mankato and work." A football lifer with high school coaching roots in addition to oil-rig boots, Nowinsky now is the coordinator sticking by Eck even as larger programs inquire about his defensive services.

item.title: For Lane Kiffin to revive LSU in CFP race, Tigers need Arch Manning injection
item.description: Lane Kiffin needs an editor. LSU recently posted on the video screens in its team facility a screed hundreds of words long that epitomized why “TLDR” (Too long, didn’t read) memes exist. What it lacked in pithiness, it compensated for in corniness and included such lines as, “When you win, everybody loves you. When you lose, everybody has an opinion.” No kidding. It read like a chatbot’s attempt at an “Us Against the World” motivational ploy and lacked authenticity. To my human brain, it read more like, “Wah, wah, we keep losing, and everybody is being so mean!” Here’s what an edited version might say: Be like Arch. Three words. One necessary mentality. Basically, Kiffin needs his team to become Arch Manning. That is, do your best work after you’re counted out. Fight hardest at the darkest hour. That’s the only way LSU can rally its way into the College Football Playoff . The task starts this weekend against suddenly hot Texas. LSU requires a dose of Arch Manning philosophy Does Kiffin need Arch as his quarterback in 2027? I've heard worse ideas. In the meantime, LSU requires an injection of the resilience Manning showed after his career and Texas’ season started walking the plank in October. Say what you will about Manning — I’ve said more than I ever planned to — just don’t say this guy has an ounce of quit in him. Dare Manning to transfer, and that’s when he’ll finally prove himself worthy of being the QB1 at a school like Texas. Just a few weeks ago, Manning was a living, breathing turnover machine , and some of his teammates appeared more interested in being content creators than serious football players. The criticism extended up to the head man. I stripped Steve Sarkisian of his “Guru Club” membership card. With Texas’ season on the brink , Manning delivered the best first half of his life against Mississippi, and the Longhorns showed a spine in some tense final moments of a season-saving win. What did Manning have to say about his rise from the ashes? Well, he darn-near thanked us for cutting him down to size and serving him the world’s biggest slice of humble pie. He dined on doubt . “I’ve been hyped up all my life,” Manning said after that Ole Miss game. “I think I kind of like being disregarded and counted out.” I wanted to know more about Arch’s thinking on this, so I asked him what’s so great about being counted out. “There's something about proving people wrong,” he said with a smile. Kiffin once experienced that. He rebuilt his career, found some peace , and tasted success like never before at Ole Miss, a place where success doesn’t always come easily. Then, after his detour in the hero’s lane, Kiffin proved the naysayers right when he burned it all down for a defector’s exit to LSU. How’s that going? item.title: Hardaway's Memphis team may offer early test for Louisville basketball
item.description: Louisville basketball agreed to a six-year series with Memphis in hopes of rekindling one of its oldest — and, at times, fiercest — rivalries. It didn't feel like one during the Cardinals' 99-73 win last December at the KFC Yum Center — their largest over the Tigers since a 95-65 beatdown Feb. 16, 1981, at Freedom Hall. Rather, it was a tale of two programs headed in opposite directions: UofL toward its first NCAA Tournament victory since 2017 and Memphis toward its worst finish in more than five decades (13-19). These aren't the same Tigers that No. 10 Louisville (2-0) will face at 1 p.m. ET Nov. 15 at FedExForum. After a 13-man roster overhaul during the offseason, coach Penny Hardaway has made quick work of restoring the positive vibes on Beale Street. Memphis is 2-1 entering the showdown against the Cards, its fourth consecutive opponent coming off a trip to March Madness this past spring. The Tigers beat then-No. 14 Iowa State 80-76 and outlasted VCU 89-88 in Week 1 before falling 105-81 at No. 19 Vanderbilt on Nov. 10. "We're going to walk into a hostile environment," coach Pat Kelsey said Nov. 7, looking forward to the matchup after UofL's win over Morehead State . "That's an unbelievable fan base there, just like Card Nation, playing in an NBA arena against a really, really high-level team." The Courier Journal caught up with The Commercial Appeal 's Memphis basketball reporter, Jason Munz , for a Q&A previewing the 92nd meeting between Louisville and the Tigers: One could make a pretty strong case for Memphis having the country's toughest opening stretch. Three games in with Penny Hardaway's 13 newcomers, what's been your biggest takeaway? Munz: The Tigers have already shown an incredible amount of resilience in a relatively short span. First, just hours before tip-off against Iowa State, they learned definitively they would be without arguably their best player, 24-year-old Serbian big man Nemanja Popovic. What do they do? item.title: East running back Evan Garrett used family motivation to rush for 1,000 yards
item.description: Evan Garrett has a little sister who is in eighth grade. When she gets to high school, she’ll have just missed her big brother, who is a senior at Pocono Mountain East and is the starting running back for the football team. Garrett had a message for his sister before the season started: Once she gets to high school, she will see her brother’s name on the wall in the gymnasium alongside every 1,000-yard rusher in school history. After the district semifinal game, Evan’s manifestation came true. He reached the milestone as the Cardinals punched their ticket to the district championship game . “It means a lot,” Garrett said. “I got to give credit to my linemen and tight ends that block for me, but I definitely showed out and did my thing.” More: East football faces biggest challenge yet in district title game vs Southern Lehigh There were some doubts about how Garrett and the East running game would look this season with the graduation of Amari Green, the electric back who was a threat to explode for a 60, 70 or 80-yard run at a moment’s notice. It was an exciting way to play the position, which left people wondering, “What will Pocono Mountain East do now?” “I heard it plenty of times – ‘You’re never going to be like Amari. He’s gone.’ ‘East isn’t going to rush for 1,000 anytime soon,’” Garrett said. “It was all just motivation for me.” Rushing for 1,000 yards is no easy feat, so Garrett did the only thing he could: Work as hard as he could. Then work some more. Garrett said he and his teammates “went through hell” in the offseason, knowing that after the departure of so many talented seniors, he would have to step up. It showed when he played. Every yard gained was a visual example of all the squats, bench presses, deadlifts, and hills with a weighted vest Garrett did throughout the summer and fall. It felt like he truly earned every one of his 1,000 yards. “Garrett’s a guy where his average is probably between 4 and 5 yards per carry, and he’s just pounding away,” head coach Dustin Thomas said. “He runs hard every single time he gets the ball.” Even with the determination to reach his goal, Garrett did it unselfishly. With the district semifinal on the line, Thomas called a run play for Garrett, but he turned it down. Instead, he opted to lead block for his teammate and quarterback Ceejay Serfass to get the rushing touchdown. “That’s about as unselfish as somebody could be on a night where you’re chasing 1,000 yards,” Thomas said. It is the 17th time a Pocono Mountain East running back ran for 1,000 yards, and Garrett is the 15th different Cardinal to reach the milestone. But he’ll be the first name little sister recognizes when she walks in the gym next school year. item.title: Ohio State needs to get Jeremiah Smith more involved in final stretch
item.description: For all the impact Ohio State has gotten from wide receiver Jeremiah Smith this season, the Buckeyes have equally suffered when failing to get the ball in his hands. During Ohio State's 41-28 loss to Oregon , Smith had seven catches on nine targets, logging 133 yards and a touchdown despite going more than 28 minutes without freshman quarterback Luke Fahey throwing in his direction. "I don't think I had the numbers in front of me, but you could feel it," Ohio State coach Ryan Day said. "There was definitely conversation on the headset. There is always conversation: 'How do we get the ball to Jeremiah?' ... When you look at how we design plays, he's obviously the first thing. We're trying to make sure he's touching the ball." Ohio State ran 26 plays during a stretch in the second and third quarter stretches in which Smith had zero targets. Fahey threw 15 passes in that time, primarily to wide receiver Devin McCuin , with a 66.7% pass completion rate (10 for 15). After Smith secured his first second-half catch, the Buckeyes posted two touchdowns and 200 total yards, 87 recorded by Smith. "There are things that are designed [for Smith], and it just doesn't go that way based on what's happening, but it's always a priority," Day said. "He's had a lot of targets, but we certainly want to give him more. There's no question. And teams do a good job on how they defend him. So when those stretches come, it's everything we can do to make sure he's touching the ball." While Smith faced multi-man coverage on some occasions against Oregon, Fahey had opportunities to connect with the team-leading receiver but instead directed his throws to McCuin, who finished with nine catches on 13 targets for 84 yards. There were also plays where Smith was on the sideline, including a third down in the second quarter. Before Ohio State second-year starting quarterback Julian Sayin suffered an apparent arm injury against Indiana on Oct. 17 , Smith was considered the front-runner for the Heisman Trophy , leading the nation in most receiving categories. Smith is tied with Oregon State's Jesse Legree for a nation-leading 14 receiving touchdowns but has fallen behind several players in receptions (69) and is second to Legree in receiving yards (1,209 compared to 1,200). The performance during the 30-18 loss to USC on Oct. 31 did little to help Jeremiah Smith, as his 10 receptions resulted in only 83 yards. However, even if Smith has a game in which he is limited in yardage, getting him the ball is still a main focal point, Ohio State offensive coordinator Arthur Smith said. "That's always a focus, every week," Arthur Smith said. "He's having a historic season. Obviously, when you lose games, we'd love to have him touch the ball every play. ... So, there are things we have to do to clean up. But that's been the focal point, every week, since I've gotten here. That will never change." bmackay@dispatch.com @brimackay15 This article originally appeared on The Columbus Dispatch: Ohio

item.title: 'Entertain always:' Banana Ball entrepreneurship explained
item.description: DAYTONA BEACH − How did a pair of sports-minded entrepreneurs start a collegiate wood-bat baseball club in 2015 and turn it into a nationwide phenomenon and franchise that today is valued at between $500 million and $1 billion? Jared Orton, president of the Savannah Bananas, listed some of the ways Nov. 10 at Daytona State College: "Make baseball fun, greatest show in sports, be fan-first, entertain always, make an impact on people." Another team mantra is a reminder that while many fans have attended multiple Bananas games, for many it's their first, so it's critical for players, ticket takers and vendors in the stands to remember that it's "someone's first game." Some 450 people, including DSC students and hundreds from Volusia and Flagler schools, heard Orton explain those concepts during the L. Gale Lemerand Entrepreneurial Speaker Series in the college's Hosseini Center. The Savannah ballclub has evolved into a professional club playing in the organization it spawned, the Banana Ball Championship League − which has flipped norms and standards, such as the untimed game, on baseball's head. The Bananas are now a traveling show, playing games to sellout crowds across the country at Yankee Stadium in New York, Wrigley Field in Chicago, and even football stadiums such as Texas A&M's Kyle Field, with a capacity of 102,000. Savannah Bananas president discusses finding the right partners Orton was a student at Belmont Abbey College in Belmont, North Carolina, when he first heard about Jesse Cole, the Bananas' cofounder. "I was on the baseball team," Orton said. "Playing was a different story." Realizing he was not going to make it in Major League Baseball, Orton said he talked to his coach about people he might approach about business opportunities in the sports world, and the coach pointed him to Cole, who was running a collegiate summer-league team. Cold-calling Cole was a lesson for Orton in getting out of his comfort zone and building relationships from scratch. "I certainly wasn't great at it, but I had to get those reps in − going out and meeting people and talking about the thing he was doing," Orton said. "Those lessons are invaluable because, to me, it was let me go work for somebody, and let me be of service to them as best as I possibly can." item.title: Offensive coordinators are the latest sacrifices delivered to angry fanbases
item.description: You can practically overlay the infamous seven stages of grief atop the various stages of heartbreak that overcomes an entire football fan base when things unravel. “Shock and denial” comes first, they say, and where do we begin in confirming that one? Ohio State and probably Oregon seem to be hanging out there these days. Pain, anger and depression line up like a Murderers Row of inevitability as losses and squeak-by wins over former doormats begin to mount, and as prized recruits and key transfers turn out to be unpredictable 20-year-olds (go figure!). In the midst of it all, along comes bargaining, which always seemed more labor-intense than mere wallowing, but different strokes, you know? What form does “bargaining” take? Well, look around. At your next red-light intersection, you might be approached by a cardboard-toting man in a headset, looking for a little help until his buyout check deposits. Offensive coordinators are the current sacrifices, and predictably, not the cheap kind you’ll find at a mid-level, off-broadway conference cellar-dweller. Jason Beck (Michigan) and Dana Holgorsen (Nebraska) are the latest to be jettisoned. Earlier, it was Drew Mehringer (Oregon) and Ben Arbuckle (Oklahoma). Presidents dump cabinet members, candidates fire campaign managers, CEOs spin the wheel and find a lower C-suite lamb to offer the unhappy masses. Head coaches on heated seats fire coordinators. At Florida (Buster Faulkner) and Ohio State (Arthur Smith), big-money coordinators are under fire just two-thirds of the way through their first seasons on the job. "Am I asking for Arthur Smith to be fired right now? Not necessarily. Just have Ryan be more involved in the offense." 🌰📉 @MattFontana83 and @jzwick12 break down whether Ryan Day needs to take back play-calling duties and how this team plans to pick up the pieces. 👇 pic.twitter.com/B1mHg2ELGI — Locked on Buckeyes (@LOBuckeyes) November 10, 2026 Some defensive coordinators were also cast aside this week: Kevin Kane (Purdue) and Jason Semore ( Georgia Tech ). While Smith remains on the job at Ohio State, Buckeyes head coach Ryan Day has been under pressure to do something/anything to temper the flaring disgust. The Buckeyes have already lost three games, something they hadn’t done in 15 years. Maybe it’s all that success that allowed Day, for now, to simply unload special-teams coach Robby Discher. All of this is cheaper than buying out the head coach, of course. And probably smarter in most cases. All in all, in its own way, it all points to one unmistakable trait of this new age of college ball. When you have to piece together, or even slap together, a new roster every spring, it’s built in large part without the cohesion gathered by two, three or four years of familiarity. There’s no way to know what you have until late November closes in and no one’s in the mood to give leeway, much less thanks. item.title: Germany boss confident Musiala will return to his best despite Hoeneß doubts
item.description: Germany boss confident Musiala will return to his best despite Hoeneß doubts Germany sporting director Rudi Völler has backed Jamal Musiala to return to top form following a series of setbacks for the Bayern Munich midfielder in recent years. Musiala missed the start of the season after suffering on-field collapses linked to a neurological condition. Upon his return, he then sustained a muscle fibre tear that has kept him sidelined for more than a month. Nevertheless, Völler has no doubts that the 23-year-old will bounce back and rediscover his best form. "Based on the information I have, I am convinced that he will come back as strong as he was before the injury. There is no reason to be sceptical about that. I am absolutely convinced that we will see Jamal Musiala in outstanding form at many, many tournaments – he is still very young, after all," Völler said on DAZN's “Never Talk Alone” programme. This season's concerns follow a horrific fibula fracture Musiala suffered after colliding with Gianluigi Donnarumma during Bayern Munich's Club World Cup quarter-final against Paris Saint-Germain in the summer of 2025. The injury kept him out of action for several months. "Unfortunately, he was also unlucky back then with Donnarumma, when he suffered a serious ankle injury and had to undergo surgery. It really was a very, very serious injury. He needs some time to get back to where he was. And if he can avoid further problems like that, I am completely optimistic that he will be able to produce top-level performances again," Völler said. Regarding Musiala's neurological condition, Völler said he would be more concerned about recurring muscle injuries. “It's not something you see every day in professional sport, but I actually thought it was a good thing that it became public and that it's being handled sensibly," he said. Bayern supervisory board member Uli Hoeneß recently described Musiala's situation as a dilemma for the club, raising doubts over whether the midfielder will ever return to his previous level. "Just imagine if Bayern Munich were now to question his contract and say: What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what is stipulated in the contract," Hoeneß told BR. Völler, however, doesn't think too much should be read into Hoeneß's comments. “I don't see it as that dramatic. These are just things – we all know Uli. Perhaps he also likes to provoke people a little in his own way. But he never really means any harm. That has always been one of his great strengths, even over all these decades: he goes out of his way to protect his own players and support them,” he said. "With one player, he might be particularly complimentary; with another, he might be a little more critical. But fundamentally, he loves them all."

item.title: St. Charles edges defending champion Jerome in boys soccer state semi
item.description: St. Charles’ biggest adjustment at halftime of a Division I boys soccer state semifinal was clogging the middle and making Dublin Jerome work on the perimeter of the field. As luck – or strategy – would have it, St. Charles ended up scoring the game’s only goal through traffic in the middle. Cardinals senior forward Sam Lofthouse punched in a shot amid a scrum in front of the net with 10:48 to play in the second half Nov. 11 at Olentangy, and a stifling defense held off the defending Division I state champions from there in a 1-0 win that put St. Charles into its second state final in four seasons. “I saw my outside back [junior Tyler Bushong] dribbling down, he crossed it in and I made a one-touch finish to the bottom corner,” Lofthouse said. “We have been talking about just putting it on frame. That’s all you can do and let the rest take care of itself.” Playing in its fourth consecutive state tournament, St. Charles (18-3-1) will face Kettering Fairmont (14-5-3) in the championship game at 7 p.m. Nov. 15 at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field. Fairmont reached its first final with a 2-1 win over Strongsville at Westerville Central. Lofthouse shifted to defense after he scored, helping St. Charles win a showdown in which it was outshot 10-7 and saw Jerome (18-3-1) put together its final serious charge with about 5 minutes left. “We decided to clog up the middle because they didn’t have many people outside,” Cardinals senior defender Tyler Stoner said. “So it would slow down the process if we had more people inside. We would have to make them change their identity and go through a different path to try to score.” Sophomore goalie Eli Wichlinski made seven saves for St. Charles, which tangled with the Ohio High School Athletic Association in September and October to play in Division I after originally being assigned to Division II. Sophomore goalie Micah Neil made three saves for Jerome. “They had more chances than us … hats off to everything they did,” St. Charles coach Chris Vonau said. “I am just super proud. We have been using the ‘climb the mountain’ slogan with everything we have been through. I am speechless, and I am never speechless about how proud I am of my guys. We made some adjustments [and] the guys bought in. They were better than us in the first half, so we had to make a move.” The Cardinals will be one of four central Ohio teams playing for state championships Nov. 15 and 16, joining CCL rival Watterson (Division III), Worthington Christian (Division IV) and Fairbanks (Division V). item.title: Dan Campbell vs Mike Vrabel: A look back at when they faced off as players
item.description: When the Detroit Lions take on the New England Patriots in Germany on Sunday, Nov. 15, it will be a head-to-head matchup of former players for their respective teams. And about 20 years ago, they went head-to-head on the field. Let's take a little walk down memory lane, back to Dec. 3, 2006, when the 2-9 Lions traveled to face the 9-2 Patriots looking to play spoilers down the stretch. They were surprisingly in the game late into the fourth quarter and had the ball with a 21-all tie and about 8:30 to go in the game. That's when Dan Campbell, playing tight end in those days, made his lone catch of the day, a 21-yard down the seam. He popped up and showed off that trademark Campbell energy with a boisterous fist pump. On the next play, though, Mike Vrabel picked off Lions quarterback Jon Kitna. It proved costly, as the Patriots survived, 28-21. The play before Vrabel's INT, Dan Campbell caught a 21-yard pass on him, despite Vrabel re-routing him up the seam. It was Campbell's only catch that day. The Pats won 28-21. https://t.co/XAe2gC4Dj0 pic.twitter.com/OIR6Li7VXk — Andrew Callahan (@_AndrewCallahan) November 11, 2026 Campbell and Vrabel won't be thumping shoulder pads in this one, but they'll still face off in a game that's important to both teams. The Lions, of course, are trying to keep pace in the highly competitive NFC North at 6-2, while the Patriots are in danger of seeing their season spiral after a shellacking from the Green Bay Packers sent them to 5-4. item.title: Why FAMU football has a score to settle with Mississippi Valley State
item.description: Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, has been circled on the calendar since Florida A&M released its 2026 football schedule. The Rattlers are seeking retribution on a team that has unexpectedly defeated it the last two seasons, Mississippi Valley State. “There is a little bit of an added motivation when it comes down to it,” said first-year FAMU head coach Quinn Fordham Gray Sr. “This team has done a good job of having our number over the last two years.” Since taking an all-time 6-0 lead over the Delta Devils, FAMU has been stunned in defeat two years in a row. The previously unheard-of wins surprised college football fans, as Valley had long been one of the Southwestern Athletic Conference’s punching bags. In November 2024, a 24-21 triumph by Mississippi Valley snapped FAMU’s sacred 23-game home winning streak on Ken Riley Field at Bragg Memorial Stadium . It spanned five seasons and was the second-longest active streak in the NCAA Division I Football Championship Subdivision. Beating FAMU was the Delta Devils only win that year and their first victory in 15 games, a losing streak dating back to the previous season. Then, in 2025, FAMU made a post-Thanksgiving trip to Itta Bena after Atlanta’s Georgia Football Classic neutral-site game was canceled due to promoter issues and was rescheduled as a normal home SWAC game. Mississippi Valley won once again 35-31. It was the final blow as FAMU decided to move on from second-year head coach James Colzie III days later . “Just understanding what they did to us in ’24, then obviously last year,” FAMU redshirt senior running back Jamal Hailey told the Tallahassee Democrat. “We got some revenge on our hearts still.” A team that was once viewed as a bye week across the SWAC now comes as a formidable opponent for the Rattlers. Early in the season, the Delta Devils pulled off an upset over current SWAC West leader Prairie View A&M, 28-27, and also beat league opponent Texas Southern 38-34. This isn’t the ‘Same old Valley,’ led by second-year head coach Terrell Buckley, a former Florida State Seminoles star returning to Tallahassee this weekend. Conversely, MVSU has an NCAA Division II loss to Delta State this year, 21-6. FAMU doesn’t know which Mississippi Valley will show up. But the goal remains the same — end a losing streak that has since cast a dark cloud over the program, as FAMU has gone 8-16 since that shocking November 2024 afternoon in Tallahassee. “They don’t lose to Valley,” said FAMU freshman quarterback Armond Parker . “Since it happened in the past two years, we got to change it.” The Week 11 FAMU-MVSU game kicks off at 3 p.m. on SWAC TV and 96.1 JAMZ . item.description: SPRINGFIELD — Missouri State men’s basketball has its sights set on next week after the Bears (3-0) defeated Division-II Newman 89-62 on Tuesday, Nov. 10.
